title: The Sharpe Pint

opening_mood.text: Morning. If you thought you could coast into the weekend on a light summer breeze, the markets have decided to throw a geopolitical hand grenade into your Friday morning coffee. Between US Marines boarding tankers in the Gulf of Oman, a brutal tech rotation that has left chip bulls crying into their flat whites, and Andy Burnham officially taking the keys to No. 10, there is plenty to unpack. Grab a pint (or a double espresso) and let's get sharp.

content.text: Uber Eats the Competition: The $14.8B Delivery Hero Takeover

Uber has agreed to acquire Germany's Delivery Hero in a massive deal valuing the firm at $14.8 billion (‐13.0 billion equity value). To dodge the antitrust police, New York-based investment firm SSW Partners is buying Delivery Hero's operations in 14 overlapping markets for $1.6 billion. This is the ultimate consolidation play. The pandemic-era delivery gold rush is long over, and now it's all about margins, scale, and cross-selling. The deal makes Uber the largest food delivery player outside China, nearly doubling its delivery footprint to 99 markets.

The City angle here is a masterclass in regulatory pre-emption. Instead of waiting for antitrust regulators to block the deal over market overlap, Uber and Delivery Hero baked a $1.6 billion divestment to SSW Partners right into the announcement. It shows how tech giants are using their massive balance sheets and stock to roll up global markets.

items: What to say at work: 'Uber's carve-out of 14 markets to SSW Partners is a masterclass in regulatory pre-emption. Instead of waiting for antitrust regulators to block the deal, they baked the divestment right into the announcement.']},{

The Great Semiconductor Selloff: AI Jitters and Geopolitical Shocks
type
paragraph
text

Global chip stocks suffered a major rout on July 16, 2026. Micron plunged 6%, Marvell fell 8.7%, and TSMC fell 5% despite reporting record earnings. Nvidia held flat (-0.28%), while megacaps like Apple, Google, and Alibaba actually rallied. It's a massive rotation. Investors are getting 'AI jitters' about the massive capital expenditure (capex) of tech giants and whether it will yield near-term returns. Plus, geopolitical tensions flared up as the US-Iran peace deal collapsed, raising fears about shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and driving up oil prices.
type
paragraph
text

This is a classic 'quality rotation.' Investors aren't abandoning AI entirely, but they are selling the high-multiple secondary chip players (Marvell, Micron, AMD) and hiding in the megacap 'buyers' of AI (Apple, Google, Alibaba) and the undisputed king (Nvidia).

What to say at work: 'TSMC's selloff despite record earnings shows the market is no longer buying the "rising tide lifts all boats" AI narrative. We're seeing a brutal rotation from secondary hardware suppliers into the actual cash-generative megacaps.'

content.text: Alibaba's Qwen Wins Apple's Blessing in China

China's Cyberspace Administration (CAC) approved Apple Intelligence for use in China. Crucially, Apple is partnering with Alibaba (integrating its Qwen LLM) and Baidu to power the AI features on iPhones, iPads, and Macs in China, rather than OpenAI's ChatGPT. Apple had to find a local partner because foreign AI models are banned in China. Alibaba's Qwen getting integrated is a massive win for Alibaba, sending its stock up over 5%.

This is a textbook example of geopolitical balkanisation in tech. The physical iPhone is global, but the 'AI brain' changes at the border. For asset managers, it highlights Alibaba's dominant position in China's enterprise AI race.

items: What to say at work: 'Apple's deal with Alibaba shows that the future of AI is going to be highly balkanised. You can't have a single global LLM stack when local regulators demand sovereign control over data and censorship.'

content.text: Eli Lilly's $3.8 Billion Psychedelic Bet

Eli Lilly agreed to acquire AtaiBeckley, a clinical-stage psychedelics developer, for up to $3.8 billion ($2.8 billion upfront in cash at $6.75/share, plus $1 billion in contingent value rights/milestones). It's the strongest sign yet that Big Pharma is fully embracing psychedelic-based medicine. AtaiBeckley's lead asset, BPL-003, is a fast-acting nasal spray based on 5-MeO-DMT for treatment-resistant depression.

Lilly is using its massive windfall profits from its weight-loss drugs (Zepbound/Mounjaro) to diversify. The deal is also boosted by a favorable regulatory shift—President Trump recently directed US regulators to expedite reviews of psychedelic treatments.

items: What to say at work: 'Lilly's acquisition of AtaiBeckley is a classic "windfall recycling" play. They're taking their massive GLP-1 cash flows and placing a high-conviction bet on the next frontier of neuroscience, backed by a friendly regulatory tailwind.'

content.text: The King of the North Takes the Crown

On Friday, July 17, 2026, Andy Burnham is officially announced as the leader of the Labour Party, clearing his final hurdle to become UK Prime Minister on Monday, July 20, following Keir Starmer's resignation. Meanwhile, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has emerged as the frontrunner to be named Chancellor, sparking a backbench revolt over her lack of economic credentials, though markets initially reacted positively to her being chosen over Ed Miliband.

Gilts outperformed European peers and sterling strengthened on Mahmood's frontrunner status, as the City prefers her perceived fiscal discipline over Miliband's. However, the backbench backlash shows Burnham faces an immediate battle to maintain party unity.

items: What to say at work: 'The market's positive reaction to Shabana Mahmood over Ed Miliband shows that the City is still deeply allergic to anything resembling loose fiscal policy. But with backbenchers already revolting over her lack of economic credentials, her honeymoon period at No. 11 will be measured in minutes, not months.'

content.text: UK Mortgages Feel the Heat from the Strait of Hormuz

At least 13 major UK lenders (including Barclays, Nationwide, NatWest, and Virgin Money) have hiked their fixed mortgage rates this week (some by up to 35 bps), reversing a recent trend of rate cuts. This comes as swap rates jumped (two-year swaps rose from 3.95% to 4.22%) due to escalating US-Iran hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz, which has virtually shut down shipping traffic (now at less than 2% of normal tonnage). It shows how geopolitical crises thousands of miles away directly impact domestic borrowing costs. Lenders aren't waiting for the Bank of England; they are repricing on swap volatility.
For fixed-income and macro traders, this is a textbook demonstration of how geopolitical risk premia feed directly into swap curves and consumer credit pricing, bypassing central bank policy rates.

items: What to say at work: 'It's a stark reminder of macro connectivity: a drone strike in the Persian Gulf translates directly into a £40-a-month hike on a semi-detached in Solihull. Lenders aren't waiting for the Bank of England; they're repricing on swap volatility.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The Morning Coffee: A Double Shot of Geopolitics and Valuation Hangovers

If you thought the summer lull was finally here, the markets had other ideas. Thursday’s session was a messy cocktail of escalating shooting wars in the Middle East and a severe valuation hangover in tech. The S&P 500 slipped 0.51% to close at 7,533.77, while the Nasdaq got thoroughly battered, sliding 1.47% to 25,882. Overnight, the pain has spread to Asia, with the Nikkei 225 diving 4% and US futures pointing to another sea of red on Friday morning. It turns out that when you mix a naval blockade in the Gulf with a sudden realization that AI infrastructure spend might actually have limits, risk appetite evaporates pretty quickly.
Equities: The AI Hangover and Netflix's Chill

The equity story is all about the chipmakers. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) dropped a monster set of results, reporting a 77% annual earnings jump. In any normal market, that’s a victory lap. Instead, its US-listed shares fell over 4%. Why? Because the market is no longer buying the 'growth at any price' narrative. Investors are looking at the eye-watering valuations of the AI complex and asking when the actual cash flows will justify them. Nvidia—now the heavy anchor of the S&P 500—fell 2.4%, while Micron plunged 5.6% and SanDisk got absolutely slaughtered, down 12.6%. To cap off a miserable 24 hours, Netflix reported after the bell. While its Q2 numbers were respectable (EPS of $0.80 beat the $0.79 consensus), its Q3 revenue guidance of $12.86 billion missed Wall Street's $13 billion target. The stock is down nearly 9% in premarket trading, proving that in this market, even a tiny guidance miss gets you taken out the back and shot.
Geopolitics: The Strait of Hormuz Goes Cold

Underpinning all of this is a massive flare-up in the Middle East. The fragile June ceasefire between the US and Iran is officially dead. Earlier this week, Washington reinstated a full naval blockade on Iranian ports, and on Thursday, US Marines boarded the tanker M/T Wen Yao in the Gulf of Oman to enforce it. With US airstrikes hitting Iranian coastal defense systems and bridges, and Iran threatening to cut off all regional energy exports, the Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed to commercial shipping. Only three commodity vessels transited the strategic waterway in a 24-hour window. Unsurprisingly, crude is on the march. Brent is trading comfortably above $85 a barrel, and WTI is hovering near $80.27. For macro desks, this isn't just a supply-chain headache; it's a major inflation shock in the making.
Rates & FX: The Warsh Effect

And that brings us to the Fed. Under new Chairman Kevin Warsh, the central bank has undergone a quiet revolution. Warsh has made it clear he wants to kill off the post-financial crisis habit of 'forward guidance'—he wants the Fed to stop hand-holding the markets. At his first FOMC meeting in June, he kept rates at 3.5%–3.75% but completely gutted the statement's dovish language. Since then, he’s been hammering the message that 'prices are too high.' With oil prices spiking due to the Hormuz crisis, the market has completely abandoned any hope of rate cuts. Instead, traders are actively pricing in rate hikes by late 2026. The US 10-year Treasury yield is creeping up toward 4.59%, and the dollar is catching a strong safe-haven bid.
Cross-Asset: Why Gold Broke Below $4,000

The most fascinating cross-asset move is in gold. Usually, when missiles start flying in the Middle East, gold is the ultimate safe haven. Yet, gold fell over 2% to break below the $4,000/oz mark, trading around $3,972. What gives? It shows that the 'higher-for-longer' rates trade is currently beating the geopolitical risk trade. Because Warsh’s Fed is expected to meet rising energy inflation with higher interest rates, the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold has spiked. It’s a classic reminder that in macro, you have to look at which narrative the marginal dollar is actually trading.
The Pub Talk: What to Say to Your VP

items: The TSMC Paradox: How to explain to a client that a company can grow earnings by 77% and still see its stock fall 4%. It’s the classic 'priced to perfection' problem—when expectations are in the stratosphere, even stellar execution is treated as a disappointment.

The Death of Forward Guidance: Kevin Warsh is deliberately making the Fed less predictable. This means macro volatility is going to stay elevated. If you're interviewing for a macro or fixed-income role, having a view on how a less-communicative Fed changes trading strategies is a great way to stand out.

The Hormuz Workarounds: While the Strait of Hormuz is blocked, keep an eye on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea pipelines and the UAE's Fujairah port. They are running at near-capacity, but they can only handle a fraction of the lost 20 million barrels a day. The energy desk is where the real action is right now.

content.text: Equity as a Call Option: The Merton Model

Imagine you buy a house for £500,000. You put down £100,000 of your own cash (equity) and take out a £400,000 interest-only mortgage (debt). If the house price shoots up to £600,000, your equity doubles to £200,000. But if the market crashes and the house is suddenly worth £300,000, you don't owe the bank £100,000 out of your pocket if you walk away—you just hand over the keys. Your maximum loss is your initial £100,000. This asymmetry is the core of corporate finance, and it is beautifully captured by the Merton Model: the idea that equity is not just "ownership", but a call option on the company’s assets.
The Mechanics: Mapping the Option
Formulated by Nobel laureate Robert Merton in 1974, the model views a firm's capital structure through the lens of option pricing. Here is how the payoff structure maps out:

items: The Underlying Asset: The total market value of the firm's operations (its assets, not just its stock price).
The Strike Price: The face value of the firm's outstanding debt.
The Expiry: The maturity date of the debt.

content.text: If, when the debt matures, the firm's assets are worth more than the debt, the equity holders "exercise" their option. They pay off the debt holders (the strike price) and keep the remaining asset value. If the assets are worth less than the debt, the equity holders default, walk away, and hand the assets over to the lenders. Because of limited liability, the equity value cannot drop below zero. The equity payoff is exactly max(V - D, 0), where V is asset value and D is debt. This is the exact payoff profile of a European call option.
Why This Matters in the City
This isn't just academic navel-gazing; it has massive practical implications for asset management, credit analysis, and special situations investing:

items: The Volatility Paradox (Wealth Transfer): Since equity is a call option, its value increases with volatility. If a highly geared company takes on a high-risk, high-reward project, the equity holders capture all the upside while the debt holders bear all the downside risk. This is a direct transfer of wealth from lenders to shareholders.

Distressed Equity as a Lottery Ticket: When a company is close to bankruptcy, its assets are worth less than its debt (the option is deep out-of-the-money). Yet, the equity price rarely hits absolute zero before filing. Why? Because of time value. If the debt matures in two years, there is still a non-zero probability that the assets will recover. The equity behaves like a highly volatile, cheap call option.

Credit Pricing (Distance to Default): Structural credit models (like the famous Moody's KMV framework) use the Merton Model in reverse. By looking at equity value and equity volatility, they back out the implied asset value and asset volatility to calculate the "Distance to Default"—giving a much more dynamic measure of credit risk than stale credit ratings.

content.text: The Classic Interview Trap
In investment banking or buy-side interviews, you might get asked: "A company has £100m of debt maturing in five years, and its assets are currently valued at £80m. What is the equity worth today?"
The amateur answer is: "Zero, because net assets are negative £20m."

The sharp answer is: "It is greater than zero. Because the debt doesn't mature for five years, the equity is an out-of-the-money call option. The equity has time value, representing the probability that the asset value will cross back above £100m before maturity."
How to Sound Smart at the Pub

Next time you are discussing a highly leveraged business that looks like a falling knife, you can say: "Stop trying to value it on a standard forward P/E. At this level of gearing, the equity is just a levered call option on their asset base. We should be pricing the option's implied volatility, not debating whether the 2027 EBITDA margin is 12% or 13%."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: If you have ever tried to explain deep hedging to a traditional options trader, you have probably met a wall of healthy skepticism. "Why would I let a black-box neural network decide my hedge ratio when I have Black-Scholes delta?" they will ask, before muttering something about transaction costs and going back to their screens. And they have a point. In the real world, continuous rebalancing is a fantasy; bid-ask spreads and fees will eat you alive. But a recent paper from researchers at Natixis and Université Paris-Dauphine PSL bridges this gap beautifully, showing how we can bake decades of stochastic control theory directly into deep learning.
The Idea: Whalley-Wilmott No-Transaction Band Networks (WW-NTBN)

Under proportional transaction costs, the optimal strategy is not to hedge continuously. Instead, as shown by Davis, Panas, and Zariphopoulou (1993), you should maintain a "no-transaction band" around your target delta. If your current hedge ratio is inside the band, you do absolutely nothing. If it drifts outside, you trade just enough to nudge it back to the boundary. In 2021, a clever architecture called the No-Transaction Band Network (NTBN) was proposed to let neural networks learn these boundaries. But it had a major flaw: it used a hard clamp function to restrict the previous hedge ratio. In deep learning, a hard clamp is a gradient killer. If your position is outside the band, the gradient with respect to the boundaries is zero, meaning the network cannot learn how to adjust them.

The paper, "Bridging Stochastic Control and Deep Hedging: Structural Priors for No-Transaction Band Networks" (March 2026), introduces the WW-NTBN. It solves the training bottleneck with three elegant tweaks: first, Delta-Centring, which explicitly centres the band on the frictionless Black-Scholes delta; second, the Whalley-Wilmott Prior, which uses the classic 1997 asymptotic formula for transaction costs to calculate a baseline bandwidth, letting the neural network simply predict a dynamic correction factor rather than learning the physics of the market from scratch; and third, the Differentiable Soft Clamp, which replaces the hard clamp with a smooth, tanh-based approximation. This keeps the gradients flowing beautifully, even when your hedge is miles out of bounds.
The Math & Code

The half-width of the classic Whalley-Wilmott band is given by w = ((3 * c * S^2 * Gamma^2) / a)^(1/3), where c is the transaction cost rate, S is the spot price, Gamma is the option's Gamma, and a is the investor's risk aversion. To make this trainable, the authors replace the hard clamp with a soft clamp: softclamp(x, l, u) = m + h * tanh(beta * (x - m) / h), where m is the midpoint of the band, h is the half-width, and beta controls the tightness. Because tanh is infinitely differentiable, gradients never vanish. Here is how you can implement this elegant hybrid in PyTorch:
Why This Matters for the Desk

items: 20x Faster Convergence: By giving the network a massive head start with the Whalley-Wilmott prior and fixing the gradient flow, training converges in seconds rather than hours.

The Bull Call Spread Breakdown: The paper uses this framework to show how price linearity breaks down under transaction costs. If you naive-hedge a bull call spread by treating the two legs independently, you trade way too much. Jointly hedging them using WW-NTBN exploits the fact that their Gammas partially cancel out, resulting in a wider band, fewer trades, and a much cheaper indifference price.

Explainability: Instead of handing a portfolio manager a black-box delta, you hand them a mathematically grounded band. They can see exactly how much of the band is driven by classical theory and how much is the neural network's empirical correction.

content.text: Pub Discussion Points & Interview Prep

items: The Physics-Informed Pitch: If you are interviewing for a quant role, this is the ultimate example of physics-informed machine learning in finance. It shows you understand that pure data-driven models are often inefficient, and the best results come from using ML to learn the residuals of classical models rather than replacing them entirely.

The Model-Agnostic Trade-off: A great discussion point with colleagues over a pint is the trade-off here. By forcing the network to centre on the Black-Scholes delta and scale with Black-Scholes gamma, you are implicitly assuming log-normal dynamics. If the market experiences a massive regime shift or jump, does the prior do more harm than good?

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Look-Ahead Trap and How to Escape It

Look-ahead bias is the silent killer of quantitative AI strategies. You build a shiny new Large Language Model pipeline, backtest it on historical data, and it looks like an absolute money-printing machine. But the moment you deploy it live, it faceplants. Why? Because the model has already 'read' the future during its massive pre-training phase, or because the market has already adapted to the very signals you are trying to exploit. It is a classic case of what academics call reflexivity.

To solve this, Ralph Koijen and Bradford Levy from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business have published a brilliant new NBER working paper. They teamed up with proprietary trading giant Optiver to launch 'Explaining Markets'—a real-time, completely out-of-sample benchmark. The goal is simple: measure how well AI systems can explain stock price moves around earnings announcements using only the information available at the exact second of the release, including the messy text of earnings call transcripts.
The Core Findings

items: Agentic AI is a massive step up: Instead of just asking an LLM for a basic sentiment score, the authors built 'agentic' systems that extract structured signals from transcripts and systematically optimise over them. The best-optimised systems more than doubled the explained variation in stock returns, pushing the R-squared from a baseline of 8% to nearly 20%.

No more black boxes: Crucially, these agents do not just spit out a raw trading signal. They generate human-readable, narrative explanations of the economic rules driving the price movements. This means portfolio managers can actually audit and understand the economic logic behind the trade.

A live playground: Along with the paper, they have released an open SDK and API, allowing researchers and quants to build their own agents and test them live on a public leaderboard against real-time market outcomes.

content.text: We find that the best-optimized systems more than double the explained variation in returns relative to standard benchmarks (R2 increasing from 8% to close to 20%). We show that AI-based optimization can deliver efficiency gains relative to traditional machine learning methods while also improving interpretability.
How to Skim This Paper

If you are short on time, skip the heavy econometrics and the formal asset pricing proofs in the middle. Focus on the introduction to understand the look-ahead problem, flip to the section detailing the 'agentic' workflow architecture to see how they structured the LLM prompts, and check out the performance charts comparing the baseline models to the optimised agents.
The Pub Talking Points

items: At the desk: 'If we are backtesting LLMs on historical earnings data, we are probably just measuring look-ahead bias. We should look at using the Koijen and Levy out-of-sample benchmark methodology to see if our text-processing models actually hold up in real-time.'

In an interview: 'The future of LLMs in quant finance isn't raw sentiment analysis. It's about agentic workflows—structuring the AI to extract clean, auditable economic rules from messy data. That is how you get the R-squared up from the single digits to around 20%, as shown in the recent Chicago Booth research.'

Over a pint: 'Optiver and Chicago Booth have basically built a live Kaggle for LLM earnings trading. If you think your prompt engineering is elite, you can download their SDK and prove it on a live leaderboard.'

content.text: The Illusion of Asymmetric Insight

Have you ever sat in a meeting, looked across the table at a counterparty or a difficult colleague, and thought: "I know exactly what makes you tick. You're just a standard-issue, risk-averse middle manager trying to protect your turf." At the exact same time, did you feel a slight pang of frustration that they couldn't possibly comprehend the deep, multi-layered strategic genius (and personal stress) behind your own proposal?
If so, welcome to the human race. You’ve just fallen headfirst into the Illusion of Asymmetric Insight.

Coined in a seminal 2001 paper by psychologists Emily Pronin, Justin Kruger, Lee Ross, and colleagues, this cognitive bias is our systematic tendency to believe we understand others far better than they understand us—and, quite often, better than they understand themselves.
The Data Asymmetry

Why do we do this? It comes down to a massive data imbalance. You have 24/7, high-definition access to your own internal monologue. You know your secret doubts, your nuanced intentions, and the complex context behind why you were ten minutes late to the morning stand-up. You are, in your own mind, a beautifully complex, soul-deep mystery.

But when you look at anyone else, you don't get their internal monologue. You only get their external behaviour. Because your brain is lazy and wants to save energy, it fills in the blanks by turning them into a flat, predictable caricature. We judge ourselves by our intentions, but others by their actions. To put it bluntly: you view yourself as a complex protagonist, and everyone else as an NPC (non-playable character).
How it plays out in the City
This illusion is the silent killer of deals, client relationships, and career progression. Here is how it manifests in the wild:

items: The "Stupid Boss" Fallacy: When a senior leader makes a decision that seems bafflingly simplistic, it’s easy to write them off as out of touch. In reality, you are likely blind to 90% of their constraints—boardroom politics, regulatory pressures, or capital allocation limits. You've simplified them, while assuming they don't "get" the complexity of your desk's daily grind.

The Deadlocked Negotiation: "We know exactly what the other side wants—they just want to squeeze us on the fee to hit their quarterly target." Meanwhile, the other side is sitting in a glass meeting room in Mayfair saying, "We know exactly what they want—they're just trying to pad their assets under management." Both sides believe they have "solved" the other, killing any chance of finding creative, non-zero-sum solutions.

The Pitch That Flops: Pitching to a new client with the attitude of "we know what your pain points are better than you do." If you treat a client like a predictable archetype, they will feel patronised and take their money elsewhere.

content.text: How to use it to your advantage
The next time you find yourself thinking you’ve completely figured someone out, pause and apply these rules:

items: Run the "NPC Check": Actively remind yourself that the person sitting across from you has an internal life just as messy, stressed, and complicated as yours. They are not a caricature.

Ask, Don't Assume: In negotiations or client pitches, replace your "insights" with genuine curiosity. Instead of saying "Since you're looking to de-risk...", ask "What are the internal pressures you're facing on risk right now?" You'll be amazed at how much gold people will give you when you stop pretending you already know the answers.

Manage Upwards with Empathy: When your boss rejects an idea, don't assume they "just don't get it." Ask: "What are the main hurdles you see from your vantage point that I might be missing?" It shows maturity, builds trust, and forces you to see the bigger picture.

content.text: One line to remember
"You are a soul-deep mystery; everyone else is a pamphlet."
